Code-mode session state and cell lifecycle ownership were split across the protocol adapter, core dispatch, and runtime actor. That made cancellation and shutdown ordering difficult to reason about, and it coupled the in-process implementation to details that a separate-process transport should not need to reproduce.

This change makes a transport-neutral `SessionRuntime` the lifecycle boundary for one code-mode session. It owns admission, shared stored values, cancellation, terminal delivery, and actor cleanup, while `CodeModeService` remains a thin protocol adapter.

Exec admission and the initial runtime response are separate events at the session boundary. A caller needs to know when a cell ID is registered and routable so it can coordinate with or terminate that cell without waiting for the first yield or terminal response.

### What changed

- `SessionRuntime` now owns the cell registry, shared stored values, root cancellation token, callback delegate, and a `TaskTracker` for actor cleanup.
- `ExecuteRequest` carries a client-provided cell ID. Core allocates compact monotonic decimal IDs that are unique within the owning session, so tracing is established before JavaScript can issue callbacks without requiring a separate dispatch-readiness gate.
- `CodeModeSession::execute` returns a `StartedCell` acknowledgement after the cell is registered and its actor is spawned. The caller awaits the initial yield or terminal response separately through `StartedCell::initial_response`.
- `CellState` is the single synchronization point for completion and termination. Its phases distinguish running work, explicit termination, committed completion, claimed completion, and closed cells.
- Stored-value writes and the transition to committed completion happen under the same phase transition. Termination cannot commit stale writes after it wins, while termination of an already-completed cell returns the committed result.
- The first terminate request atomically claims a buffered completion. A second terminate request receives `AlreadyTerminating` instead of consuming the same result again.
- Cancellation flows from the session token to each cell and then to its notification and tool callbacks. Callback wrappers stop awaiting non-cooperative delegate futures after cancellation.
- Natural completion drains notifications before committing the result, then cancels remaining tool callbacks. Explicit termination and session shutdown cancel both callback classes before publishing the terminal outcome.
- Shutdown cancels the session first, serializes with cell admission through the registry lock, closes the task tracker, and waits for actor cleanup. Dropping the session initiates the same cancellation without waiting.
- Closed cell IDs become registry tombstones for the remainder of the session, preventing ID reuse while releasing the actor handle and its retained output.
- Core no longer maintains per-cell dispatch gates. Its turn worker dispatches callbacks only while the cell cancellation token remains live.

### Cell lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Running
    Running --> Terminating: explicit terminate
    Running --> Completed: result commit
    Running --> Tombstone: session cancellation
    Completed --> CompletionClaimed: terminate buffered result
    Completed --> Tombstone: observer delivery or shutdown
    CompletionClaimed --> Tombstone: actor cleanup
    Terminating --> Tombstone: runtime and callback cleanup
    Tombstone --> [*]
```

`CellState` is authoritative for the terminal outcome. Cancellation tokens wake asynchronous work, while the state transition determines whether completion or termination won. The registry retains a separate lightweight tombstone after actor cleanup so a client-provided ID cannot be reused within the same session.

### Tests

Coverage includes acknowledgement before the initial response, termination after acknowledgement, admission versus shutdown ordering, termination during completion commit, session shutdown during callback cleanup, cancellation of non-cooperative callbacks, abandoned-observer completion buffering, single-consumer buffered completion, session drop, and preservation of client-provided cell IDs.

### Out of scope

- This PR establishes the transport-neutral runtime contract; it does not move execution into a separate process.
- Bounding output retained by cells that are never observed remains a follow-up.

This is part 2 of an eight-PR stack that prevents concurrent MCP OAuth refreshers from replaying a rotating refresh token or overwriting newer credentials.

## Review order

1. [openai/codex#29017](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29017) — refresh transaction and lifecycle-local store pinning
2. **[openai/codex#29020](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29020) — authoritative reread after lock acquisition (this PR)**
3. [openai/codex#29019](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29019) — serialize login and logout with refresh
4. [openai/codex#29021](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29021) — lock aggregate File and Secrets stores
5. [openai/codex#30090](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/30090) — retain refreshed credentials after a persistence failure
6. [openai/codex#30091](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/30091) — add Codex-owned proactive and 401 recovery
7. [openai/codex#29018](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29018) — make Codex the exclusive refresh owner for all RMCP traffic
8. [openai/codex#30089](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/30089) — end-to-end transport recovery coverage

## Why this layer exists

Serialization alone is insufficient if a waiter decides from credentials it read before acquiring the lock. The first process may already have rotated A to B. A later waiter must reread the selected durable store after it owns the transaction and adopt B instead of sending A to the provider again.

## What changes

- Reread the lifecycle-pinned credential store only after acquiring the per-credential transaction lock.
- Adopt a newer durable credential snapshot into the authorization manager and skip the duplicate provider refresh.
- Treat confirmed deletion as authoritative rather than resurrecting the caller's stale in-memory credentials.
- Propagate read failures from the selected store; do not consult the other `Auto` store.

## Decisions reviewers should preserve across the stack

- `Auto` resolution is lifecycle-local and not durably persisted. Once resolved, the client never hot-switches stores.
- The post-lock reread, not the caller's pre-lock snapshot, is authoritative unless a later layer has an unpersisted successful refresh in memory.
- Provider timeout releases the lock with an unknown outcome and allows a later serialized retry.
- In the final stack, public request/notification recovery remains at `RmcpClient`; RMCP-owned response/GET/DELETE recovery lives in the transport wrapper.
- The original [openai/codex#28647](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28647) and its branch are untouched.

## Review focus

Review the ordering: acquire transaction lock, reread the already-resolved store, adopt/clear/refresh, then persist before release. This PR does not change login/logout yet.

## Non-goals

- Durable `Auto` selection, cross-`CODEX_HOME` keyring coordination, or backend migration.
- Login/logout serialization; that is part 3.

## Validation

- `just test -p codex-rmcp-client`: 100 passed, 5 skipped.
- Cross-client coverage proves only one provider refresh occurs and the waiter adopts the winner.

## Why

Every turn resolves a skills snapshot before model work starts. Previously, `snapshot_for_config()` discovered skill roots before checking the process-wide cache. Even when the snapshot was already cached, the turn still walked cwd ancestors for project markers and checked candidate `.agents/skills` directories. Those metadata operations can noticeably delay turn startup on slow or remote filesystems.

Returning from the cache before root discovery removes that per-turn I/O, but it also means filesystem-derived roots need an explicit refresh boundary. Otherwise, a repo `.agents/skills` root created after the first lookup could remain invisible for the lifetime of the process.

## What changed

The config-aware cache now uses a skill-relevant, in-memory request key, so normal turn lookups can return a cached snapshot without touching the environment filesystem. Cache entries also retain a fingerprint of the resolved roots and skill configuration rules.

Conversation initialization explicitly refreshes that fingerprint. If the roots and rules are unchanged, it reuses the complete snapshot without rescanning skill contents. If they changed, it rebuilds the snapshot. This makes a newly created repo `.agents/skills` root visible by the next conversation while keeping the per-turn path free of filesystem work.

Plugin skill snapshot ownership, watcher behavior, and existing explicit cache invalidation remain unchanged. Changes inside an already discovered root continue to use those existing invalidation paths.

## Testing

- `just test -p codex-core-skills` (108 passed)
- Added regression coverage showing that cache hits perform no environment filesystem operations, an unchanged conversation-start refresh avoids rescanning skill contents, and a newly created repo `.agents/skills` root is discovered by refresh.

## Why

The app-server integration needs Codex's RPC and telemetry dependencies to share the monorepo's Tonic and Prost versions. Keeping the newer versions created a separate Tokio dependency universe at that integration boundary, which can produce runtime-context panics.

## What Changed

- Downgrade direct Tonic usage to `0.12.3` and Prost usage to `0.13.5`.
- Replace `tonic-prost` generation with `tonic-build` and regenerate the config protobuf bindings.
- Align OpenTelemetry with the compatible dependency line and port the affected metric and OTLP code.
- Allow `axum` and `axum-core` as transitive `async-trait` wrappers introduced by Tonic `0.12`.
- Refresh the Cargo and Bazel module lockfiles.

## Downgrade Impact

The thread-config protobuf schema and unary RPC method are unchanged, so the app-server integration remains wire-compatible.

The main tradeoff is telemetry. Compared with OpenTelemetry `0.30` and `0.31`, Codex gives up the default metric cardinality cap, context-based suppression that prevents recursive exporter telemetry, improved remote-parent span flags, and fixes to batch-export parallelism. Codex does not call those newer APIs today, but they are useful upstream safety and correctness improvements.

Tonic `0.14` improvements are not used by Codex's current RPC path: newer routers, health/watch APIs, TCP keepalive controls, TLS handshake timeouts, and load shedding. Its decompression message-size fix is also inactive because Codex does not configure gRPC compression.

Prost `0.14` adds build and type-generation improvements that Codex does not use. The observable local difference is that some private generated thread-config message types no longer derive `Eq` and `Hash`; no call site depends on those traits.

Upstream references: [OpenTelemetry SDK 0.30](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust/blob/v0.31.0/opentelemetry-sdk/CHANGELOG.md#0300), [OpenTelemetry SDK 0.31](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust/blob/v0.31.0/opentelemetry-sdk/CHANGELOG.md#0310), [Tonic 0.14](https://github.com/hyperium/tonic/releases/tag/v0.14.0), and [Prost 0.14](https://github.com/tokio-rs/prost/releases/tag/v0.14.1).

Sandboxed servers bind inside Codex's Linux sandbox network namespace, so callers outside that namespace cannot reach them through the executor host's normal network namespace.

## Why

When the token-budget feature is enabled, compaction should behave like the `new_context` tool: start a fresh context window with the normal injected context, without asking the server to compact history and without carrying prior user or assistant transcript messages forward. That keeps token-budget windows explicit and avoids summarizing old conversation state into the next window.

At the same time, this is still a compaction operation from the client lifecycle perspective. Compact hooks and `TurnItem::ContextCompaction` events need to fire so callers that observe compaction side effects do not have to special-case token-budget resets.

One important exception is mid-turn auto-compaction while the model still has an active follow-up, such as pending tool output. Resetting the window at that point can discard continuation state, so token-budget compaction now lets the active follow-up finish and relies on the pre-turn compaction path to reset before the next user turn if the budget is still exhausted.

Note: `NewContextWindowMode` keeps forced resets distinct from request-driven resets at the call site. Token-budget compaction uses `ForceStart` because the compaction operation itself is the request to reset context, while the `new_context` tool path uses `StartIfRequested` to consume a pending request.

## What changed

- Added a shared `start_new_context_window` path that installs the standard injected context, world-state baseline, rollout metadata, token recomputation, and previous-turn settings.
- Made new-context window startup explicit at call sites with `NewContextWindowMode::ForceStart` and `NewContextWindowMode::StartIfRequested`, so callers choose whether to force a fresh window or only honor a pending request.
- Added a token-budget compaction helper that runs compact hooks, emits `ContextCompaction` item start/completion events, and installs a fresh context window without local or remote summarization.
- Routed token-budget manual `/compact` and inline auto-compaction resets through that helper.
- Kept pending `new_context` request handling explicit before auto-compaction, so request-driven resets are consumed before forced token-budget compaction.
- Deferred token-budget mid-turn auto-compaction when the model still needs follow-up, preserving active tool-call continuation state.
- Ensured token-budget model-switch resets use the current turn context and do not duplicate model-switch context.
- Updated rollout reconstruction so compact reset segments can rehydrate both the reference context and previous-turn settings after resume.
- Extended token-budget integration coverage for fresh-window compaction, auto/manual compact hooks, `ContextCompaction` events, active follow-up preservation, model-switch resets, and compact-reset rollout reconstruction.

## Why

A selected executor may become ready between two model calls. Its skills should appear on the next call, and the catalog shown to the model must match the filesystem used to read the selected skill.

Today host, executor, and orchestrator skills can be listed and selected by different paths. That makes name collisions hard to reason about and can inject two different skills for one `$name`.

## What changed

- Build one immutable `SkillsSnapshot` for every `StepContext`.
- Merge host skills, ready selected-executor skills, and the optional orchestrator source into that snapshot.
- Keep every entry bound to the exact source that listed it.
- Make World State own the single complete skills catalog and emit a replacement only when it changes.
- Use one selector and one injection path for every source.
- Remove the extension's parallel catalog and turn-input injection path; it still owns orchestrator transport and the explicit `skills.list` / `skills.read` tools.
- Keep skill dependency setup and skill-linked connector refresh in the same step before sampling.
- Keep the stable usage policy once; later World State updates replace only the complete catalog.
- When a new source replaces an already-injected skill with the same name, mark the new body as the authoritative replacement.

## Selection rule

An exact locator always wins. A plain name uses this order:

```text
selected executor > orchestrator > host
```

If two skills tie inside the winning source, Codex asks for an exact locator instead of picking one arbitrarily.

Example:

```text
host:         deploy -> /repo/.codex/skills/deploy/SKILL.md
orchestrator: deploy -> skill://orchestrator/deploy/SKILL.md
executor:     deploy -> skill://demo-plugin@1/skills/deploy/SKILL.md

$deploy                                      -> executor skill
skill://orchestrator/deploy/SKILL.md         -> orchestrator skill
/repo/.codex/skills/deploy/SKILL.md          -> host skill
```

## Dynamic example

```text
step 1: selected executor is pending
        -> $deploy lists and reads the host skill

user steers: "Use $deploy once it is available"
executor becomes ready

step 2: a fresh snapshot sees the exact ready executor
        -> World State replaces the catalog with executor $deploy
        -> the new body is read through that captured executor filesystem
        -> it explicitly replaces the earlier host instructions
        -> it is injected once before sampling
```

Catalog metadata stays byte-bounded. Each step can inject at most 8 new skill bodies and 32 KB total. A genuinely replaced executor gets a new source identity; a transport reconnect to the same executor object does not.

This cutover removes the old extension owner and its parallel tests in the same PR. Most of the large diff is that deletion. Splitting it further would leave two catalogs active at once, which is harder to understand and easier to get wrong.

MCP servers and connectors are intentionally handled by the next two PRs.

## Why

Codex currently reads the session's latest MCP manager in several places. A model request can therefore advertise a tool from manager A, then execute the call through manager B if a refresh happens in between.

One model step needs one coherent MCP view.

## What changed

- Pair the effective `McpConfig`, runtime context, and `McpConnectionManager` in one immutable `McpRuntimeSnapshot`.
- Attach that snapshot to `StepContext`.
- Use the step snapshot for model-visible tool discovery, connector attribution, MCP calls, resource tools, approvals, and execution metadata.
- Publish refreshed config + manager pairs together for future steps.
- Build both halves of a refresh from the same effective `Config`, including dependencies installed by a selected skill.
- Let out-of-band APIs use the latest published snapshot.
- Keep a superseded manager alive while an in-flight step still owns it.
- If a skill installs an MCP dependency before sampling, update only this step's MCP view; keep its captured environment, roots, and skills unchanged.
- Use the same snapshot for thread-scoped HTTP/OAuth resolution, so auth cannot combine one config with another runtime context.

## Example

```text
step captures runtime A
  -> advertises mcp__build__run from A

session refresh publishes runtime B

model calls mcp__build__run for the in-flight step
  -> execution still uses A

next model step
  -> captures B
```

The connector list used for skill collisions and skill-linked apps also comes from this exact snapshot, rather than a turn-start copy.

5. **[openai/codex#30090](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/30090) — retain refreshed credentials after a persistence failure (this PR)**
6. [openai/codex#30091](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/30091) — add Codex-owned proactive and 401 recovery

## Why this layer exists

After the provider successfully rotates A to B, B is the only potentially usable credential even if durable persistence fails. Reinstalling durable A on the next operation would discard B and replay an already-consumed refresh token.

## What changes

- Make refreshed B authoritative in the authorization manager and the persistor's in-memory state before attempting the durable write.
- Record that B has not been persisted and retain the last credential snapshot known to be durable.
- Keep healthy access-token requests on B for the current process.
- On B's next refresh, reread under the transaction lock only to reconcile authority: unchanged durable A fails closed, while a serialized login, logout, or concurrent refresh that replaced A is adopted.
- Add structured stage and timing logs for provider refresh and persistence failures.

## Decisions reviewers should preserve across the stack

- A successful provider response transfers in-process authority to B before persistence.
- This stack intentionally does not retry persistence, in the foreground or background. The error is logged and returned so telemetry can tell us whether a retry policy is needed.
- A healthy B may continue serving requests without polling durable storage on every operation. When B itself needs refresh, unchanged durable A returns the pending-persistence error; a credential that changed under the shared transaction lock is authoritative and may be adopted.
- Provider timeout is different: no B was received, so the outcome remains unknown and a later serialized retry is allowed.
- `Auto` remains lifecycle-local and never hot-switches after construction.
- The original [openai/codex#28647](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28647) and its branch are untouched.

## Review focus

Review the authority transition around the fallible save, the retained last-known-durable snapshot, and the distinction between “provider response succeeded, persistence failed” and “provider outcome unknown.” No transport ownership changes occur in this layer.

## Non-goals

- Retrying failed persistence.
- Quarantining credentials after provider timeout.
- Durable `Auto` selection or backend migration.

- `just test -p codex-rmcp-client`: 108 passed, 5 skipped.
- Regression coverage proves an unchanged stale durable snapshot is never reinstalled after a failed save.

## Why

Executor skill discovery uses the optimized `fs/walk` RPC. A newer Codex client can still connect to an exec-server that does not expose that RPC yet.

Before this change:

```text
selected environment is ready
  -> skills call fs/walk
  -> older exec-server returns method not found
  -> the thread caches an empty executor skill catalog
```

This is what the selected-capability integration test exposed: MCP was available, but the skill catalog stayed empty.

## What changed

Remote filesystem walks still use `fs/walk` normally. Only when the server returns the JSON-RPC “method not found” error, the client performs the same bounded walk through the older primitive filesystem operations (`fs/readDirectory`, `fs/getMetadata`, and `fs/canonicalize`).

```text
fs/walk supported     -> one optimized RPC
fs/walk unsupported   -> bounded compatibility walk
any other error       -> unchanged error behavior
```

The fallback reuses the existing filesystem walk implementation, including its depth, directory, entry, and response-size limits.

This does not change skill caching, World State, environment readiness, or MCP runtime behavior. It only preserves remote filesystem walking across app-server/exec-server version skew.
